metadata.title: Skill Mismatch and Public Policy in OECD Countries (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses microdata from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) conducted in 2011-12 across 22 OECD countries, but the working paper does not report the use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight procedures in the empirical specification. The models are pooled cross-country logit regressions where the dependent variable is a binary indicator of skill mismatch (over- or under-skilled) and the regressors include individual/job characteristics plus country-level policy indicators. Because the paper does not document whether PIAAC sampling weights (e.g., student/sampling weights) were applied, the safest interpretation is that results are based on the available analytic sample without explicit weight handling. Analysts should therefore treat the reported cross-country marginal effects as descriptive correlations unless weighting and design-based variance estimation are confirmed in the underlying OECD/PIAAC data documentation.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is a binary skill-mismatch indicator derived from PIAAC literacy proficiency scores combined with self-assessed mismatch and occupation-specific thresholds; the paper does not describe plausible-value (PV) generation/combining or whether PVs were used in the mismatch construction. Missing-data handling is also not documented (e.g., whether cases with missing covariates were excluded or imputed), which is a reporting gap for reproducibility. Given the paper’s focus on policy correlations using a constructed mismatch measure rather than reporting PV-based achievement models, PV handling is treated as not applicable at the level of the reported empirical specification.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PIAAC microdata for adults aged 16-65 from 22 OECD countries (2011-12). Skill mismatch is constructed using the OECD approach that combines self-reported mismatch with literacy proficiency scores and occupation-specific thresholds based on percentiles (the analysis uses 10th/90th percentile thresholds as stated in Box 1). The empirical models are pooled cross-country logit regressions that include individual characteristics (age categories, gender, nationality/foreign-born, marital status, education level, firm size, contract type, full-time employment, and private-sector vs public/NGO) and then augment with country-level policy indicators; the paper does not specify additional task/module completion filters beyond the mismatch construction requirements.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper uses PIAAC 2011-12 microdata for adults aged 16-65 in 22 OECD countries to study how policy environments relate to skill mismatch, defined as over- or under-skilling using an OECD construction that combines self-assessment with literacy proficiency thresholds by occupation. The empirical strategy estimates pooled cross-country logit models: first, mismatch is regressed on individual and job characteristics; then country-level policy indicators are added one at a time to avoid multicollinearity, and finally interaction models test heterogeneous effects for youth. The paper reports marginal effects and average effects (log-odds) with statistical significance, including economically meaningful scenario changes (e.g., bankruptcy cost reductions and housing transaction cost reductions). It does not report ML performance metrics (AUC/RMSE) and explicitly cautions that results are bivariate correlations rather than causal estimates due to cross-sectional data and policy endogeneity concerns.
